proof_skeleton_nl: Fix arbitrary integers m >= 2 and g >= 0. Use the Kunz-coordinate bijection to translate numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g into the coordinate layer K_{m,g}, and similarly translate genus g+1 semigroups into K_{m,g+1}. Prove both coordinate layers are finite. Invoke the hard coordinate-layer monotonicity lemma giving an injection K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1}. Apply the finite-set injection principle to deduce |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}|. Finally replace these cardinalities by N(m,g) and N(m,g+1) via the bijection lemma. Since m and g were arbitrary, the desired inequality holds for all m >= 2 and g >= 0.

steps.derives: Fix integers m >= 2 and g >= 0. If A_{m,g} is the set of numerical semigroups S with multiplicity m(S)=m and genus g(S)=g, if N(m,g)=|A_{m,g}|, and if K_{m,g} is the set of positive integer tuples satisfying the Kunz inequalities and having coordinate sum g, then N(m,g)=|K_{m,g}|.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the concluding sentence of L5.

steps.derives: For the same fixed integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, if K_{m,g+1} is defined by the same Kunz inequalities together with coordinate sum g+1, then N(m,g+1)=|K_{m,g+1}|.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L5 with the genus parameter replaced by g+1; the hypothesis g >= 0 implies g+1 >= 0.

steps.derives: For the fixed integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, the set K_{m,g} is finite.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the assertion of L6.

steps.derives: For the same fixed integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, the set K_{m,g+1} is finite.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L6 with the genus parameter replaced by g+1.

steps.derives: For the fixed integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, there exists an injective function Phi_{m,g} : K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1}.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the assertion of L7.

From A3 and A4, both K_{m,g} and K_{m,g+1} are finite. From A5, there is an injective function from K_{m,g} to K_{m,g+1}. Applying L8 to these two finite sets and this injection yields the cardinality inequality |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}|.
A1 identifies N(m,g) with |K_{m,g}|. A2 identifies N(m,g+1) with |K_{m,g+1}|. Substituting these equalities into the inequality from A6 gives N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= 0, the number N(m, g) of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g satisfies N(m, g) <= N(m, g + 1).
steps.trivial_justification: The argument in A1-A7 was carried out for arbitrary fixed integers m >= 2 and g >= 0. Therefore universal generalization yields exactly the stated theorem.
